headline: Library Digitization Project Uncovers 1923 Article About Hartwell Construction: 'Building Rose Overnight'
subheadline: Newspaper clipping describes 14-story building appearing 'between sunset and sunrise'; architect quoted saying 'it was always here'
summary: A newly digitized 1923 newspaper article contradicts official records about the Hartwell Building's construction timeline.
content:
The City Library's ongoing newspaper digitization project has uncovered a 1923 article that raises disturbing questions about the Hartwell Building's origins.

The article, published in the now-defunct City Evening Herald on March 14, 1923, describes local residents' reaction to the sudden appearance of the Hartwell Building at its current location.

"FOURTEEN STORIES RISE OVERNIGHT," the headline reads. "Citizens Report Building 'Simply Appeared' Where Empty Lot Stood Yesterday."

The article quotes several witnesses:

"I walked past that lot every day for years," said Mrs. Eleanor Hutchins, a resident of nearby Maple Street. "Tuesday evening, it was empty. Wednesday morning, there was a building. A completed building. With people going in and out like it had always been there."

The building's architect, William Hartwell, was reached for comment. His response, as quoted in the article, is particularly troubling: "The building was not constructed. The building was revealed. It was always here. We simply removed what was covering it."

Two weeks after the article's publication, William Hartwell died in what the Herald called "circumstances too distressing to print." No further details were provided, and no obituary has been located.

The 1923 article contradicts all official records, which describe a conventional 18-month construction process beginning in 1921. Building permits, contractor invoices, and inspection reports all support the official timeline.

Library archivist Grace Nomura, who discovered the article, has her doubts about the official version.

"I've been digitizing papers from this era for eight months," Nomura said. "There are 47 articles about the Hartwell Building from 1921-1923. Forty-six of them describe normal construction. This one doesn't. And here's the strange part: this one is dated two months before the official completion date."

Omnicorp Holdings, which has owned the building since 1923, declined to comment on the article. A spokesperson noted only that "historical newspaper reporting often contained inaccuracies" and that "the official construction records are the definitive account."

The original newspaper archive, housed in the library's basement, was scheduled for further examination. However, the specific volume containing the March 1923 edition was reported missing the day after Nomura's discovery.

"It was there Monday," Nomura said. "It was gone Tuesday. The checkout log shows no record of anyone accessing it. But someone left a business card where the volume used to be."

The card bore the Omnicorp Holdings logo and a single handwritten message: "Some things are archived for a reason. Thank you for your understanding."

Dr. Elena Martinez, when shown a digital copy of the 1923 article, declined to comment but was observed booking a flight that evening. Her destination was not disclosed.
author: Tom Hendricks, City Hall Reporter
